description: In this project, we have designed an interactive website that explores the scientific similarities between Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Users can discover and compare similar locations through 3D globes, real images, geographical information, and scientific charts.We have also included educational games, space quizzes, and creative activities, such as designing and building your own rocket. Our goal is to make space science simple, exciting, and accessible to everyone, especially children.
summary: AETHER NOVA is an interactive browser-based comparative planetology explorer connecting 9 Martian regions and 7 lunar sites with 21 documented terrestrial analogs on Earth. Users rotate interactive 3D-style celestial globes, inspect side-by-side geological and mineralogical profiles, compare reference elevation and surface gravity charts, view curated NASA orbital and Earth imagery, and check modeled Earth weather forecasts. To make planetary science accessible to students and younger learners, the platform also integrates interactive matching and memory games, picture stories, a space mission drawing studio, a digital rocket builder, and a timed science quiz across a 20-language interface. By explicitly distinguishing specific geological process analogies—such as carbonate shorelines, sulfate evaporites, shield volcanism, impact craters, and periglacial terrain—from full planetary equivalence, AETHER NOVA helps learners and researchers explore how Earth field sites inform Mars and Moon exploration.
details:
Problem & Challenge Connection

Planetary surfaces on Mars and the Moon are distant and difficult to interpret without familiar terrestrial context, yet comparing off-world landforms with Earth sites can easily mislead learners if scale and planetary differences are ignored. AETHER NOVA addresses this challenge by pairing 9 documented Martian regions and 7 lunar sites with 21 terrestrial analog locations on Earth, explicitly clarifying which specific geological, geochemical, or morphological processes are comparable and where planetary conditions differ.

Current Capabilities

- Curated Comparative Catalog: Connects 9 Martian features (Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Hellas Planitia, Gusev Crater, Utopia Planitia, Elysium Volcanic Province, and Isidis Planitia / Nili Fossae) and 7 lunar features (Copernicus Crater, Mare Tranquillitatis, Shackleton Crater, Aristarchus Plateau, Hadley Rille, Tycho Crater, and Marius Hills) with primary and secondary Earth analogs (such as Lake Salda, Lut Desert, Salar de Pajonales, Mauna Loa, Danakil Depression, Death Valley, Río Tinto, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Holuhraun, Namib Sand Sea, Samail Ophiolite, Meteor Crater, Pingualuit Crater, Kīlauea, Cinder Lake, and Lava Beds). Each pair includes evidence confidence levels and process-specific explanations.

- Interactive Celestial Globes: Three HTML5 Canvas interactive globes for Earth, Mars (referencing NASA Mars Trek), and the Moon (referencing NASA Moon Trek) supporting drag rotation, zoom controls, and click-based selection of the nearest catalog site.

- Geographic Profiles & Scientific Charts: Side-by-side comparison of coordinates, reference elevations, landform types, mineral assemblages, mission context, surface gravity, and atmospheric summaries, accompanied by Canvas bar charts comparing reference elevation and surface gravity plus a 7-day Earth analog temperature forecast chart powered by Open-Meteo and NASA POWER climatology endpoints.

- Curated Visual Atlases & Offline Fallbacks: Source-linked NASA Earth Observatory, JPL Photojournal, SVS, and LPI imagery with a full-screen lightbox viewer, paired with clearly labeled offline schematic illustrations ("not an actual photograph") when internet access is unavailable.

- Interactive Educational & Youth Studio: Includes a 6-badge Mission Hub, a Mars-to-Earth line-matching game, a 5+5 visual comparison browser, a 10-card offline memory game with scientific explanations, 5 illustrated comparison stories, a 5-word sentence builder, a free-form space mission drawing canvas with 12 rotatable/scalable exploration stamps, a drag-and-drop digital rocket builder with JSON save/load, and a 20-question timed Space Explorer quiz.

- Multilingual Interface: Includes a 20-language selector covering core navigation and interface labels alongside full Persian and English localization for the primary scientific catalog.

Tools, Languages & Creativity

AETHER NOVA is built as a lightweight, zero-install browser application using HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript, utilizing HTML5 Canvas for interactive globes, scientific charts, the drawing studio, and the rocket builder, alongside Leaflet stylesheets and Google Fonts (Vazirmatn and Outfit). Its creative approach bridges rigorous comparative planetology—distinguishing process analogies from identical twins—with hands-on interactive games and creative mission-design tools for younger learners.

Intended Impact & Limitations

The platform is designed as a free educational and exploratory reference for students, educators, and space enthusiasts. Key limitations include:

- Process-Only Analogy: Terrestrial sites represent specific geological or environmental processes (e.g., carbonate precipitation, basaltic shield volcanism, impact excavation, or periglacial ground) rather than full scale, gravity, or atmospheric equivalence.

- Reference vs. Live Data: Planetary elevations, temperatures, and pressures are broad contextual reference values rather than real-time local sensor telemetry; lunar entries have no local elevation values in the catalog and no Earth-like weather. Live Earth forecasts, climatology, and remote archival images require an active internet connection and third-party API availability.

- Language Coverage: While the interface provides a 20-language switcher, several interactive youth and storytelling sections are currently authored primarily in Persian.
